habitat: Foxface rabbitfish inhabit coral reefs and lagoons of the Western Pacific, from southern Japan through the Philippines and Indonesia to the Great Barrier Reef. They are found at depths of 5-30 meters, frequenting outer reef slopes, coral-rich lagoons, and seagrass beds. They are diurnal, spending daylight hours foraging and seeking shelter among coral heads and crevices at night. Their bold black, white, and yellow facial patterning — resembling a fox's face — provides camouflage among the dappled light of reef environments.
diet: Foxface rabbitfish are primarily herbivorous, feeding on various species of algae (including troublesome hair algae that plague reef aquariums), seagrass, and occasionally sponges and tunicates. They play a crucial ecological role in controlling algal growth on coral reefs, preventing algae from overgrowing corals. In captivity, they accept a wide variety of prepared foods including nori (dried seaweed), spirulina flakes, and fresh vegetables. They have specialized teeth for scraping algae from rock surfaces.
behavior: Foxface rabbitfish are peaceful, shy fish that prefer the security of rock crevices and coral overhangs. When threatened, they undergo a dramatic color change — their bright yellow fades to a mottled brown-black pattern — and they erect their venomous dorsal spines as a defense. They are monogamous and often seen in pairs. Their venomous spines (13 dorsal, 7 anal, 4 pelvic) deliver a painful sting comparable to a bee sting, though they only use them defensively and are not aggressive toward humans. At night, they settle into crevices, sometimes adopting a head-down posture.
facts: The foxface rabbitfish gets its name from its elongated snout and distinctive facial pattern — a bold black-and-white band that resembles a fox's face. They can rapidly change between their bright day coloration and a camouflaged brown night pattern. Adults reach 22-25 cm. Their venomous spines are grooved with venom glands along each side — painful but not life-threatening to humans. They are among the most popular marine aquarium fish for their beauty, peaceful nature, and algae-eating services. The species name 'vulpinus' means 'fox-like.'
naming: Foxface names might reflect their fox-like appearance or marine habitat. Consider names like Foxy, Zorro, Reef, Algae, Coral, Spike, Nori, Sushi, Vulpes (Latin for fox), or Laguna.
